transcript.content:
I know it sounds odd, but it would quietly make my day if the Moon happened to be impossible to see right now.

I'm in Edinburgh, Scotland, UK at 2026-09-29 19:59 BST (UTC+0100) (2026-09-29T18:59:00Z in UTC), at latitude 55.9533 degrees and longitude -3.1883 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -9.415 degrees and its azimuth is 280.21 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 5.272 degrees and its azimuth is 59.687 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 88.2 percent illuminated, 139.714 degrees from the Sun, and 370221.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is nautical twilight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—almost certainly.

An **88.2%-illuminated Moon** is extremely bright. At **5.27° altitude** it is low in the **northeast (azimuth ≈60°)**, so atmospheric extinction and haze will dim it somewhat, but not remotely enough to hide it in a **clear nautical-twilight sky**. With the Sun **9.4° below the horizon**, the sky is already fairly dark.

The main obstacle is geometric: from Edinburgh, buildings, trees, hills, or local haze could block the view only **five degrees above the horizon**. Atmospheric refraction may also shift its apparent position slightly upward, depending on whether your app reports geometric or apparent altitude.

So, with a genuinely clear and unobstructed northeastern horizon, you should be able to spot it easily with unaided eyes. It would be “impossible to see” only if foreground obstructions or a low cloud/haze bank concealed it—not because of its brightness or phase.
